news.title: Why are bond yields surging, and why does it matter?
news.summary:
STORY: "Why are bond yields up so much at the moment, at multi-decade highs in some cases?"

:: Singapore / August 19, 2026

:: Gregor Stuart Hunter, Asia Finance and Markets Correspondent

"At risk of giving an overly simple answer, it essentially boils down to there being fewer buyers than sellers. But what do I mean by that? Okay, so right now, bond investors are looking at the ballooning government deficits across the developed world in places like the US and Japan and Europe, and they're demanding additional compensation to part with their money and lend to these governments. At the same time, because the conflict in the Middle East remains at stalemate and oil prices are going up, there's an expectation that inflation is going to be higher for longer and that's going to further erode the kind of returns that bond investors are used to getting. So in turn, they're going to demand more compensation for that. That's why bond yields are going up all over the world."

"So a new source of supply for the bond markets over the last few years has been from the global tech sector. Companies like Microsoft, Amazon // these companies have all been deploying tens of billions, in some cases hundreds of billions of dollars of capital to buy chips, data centers // and having funneled most of their free cash flows into this investment, they're now taking on more and more debt to fund that expansion. And that's competing with traditional sources of bonds like banks and government debt. So there are increasing sources of supply and just not enough money to go around."

:: Federal Reserve Board

"So government borrowing costs going up have a whole host of implications because the more money that governments are funneling towards interest payments, the less they have available for things like defense, social services."

"But also bear in mind that the same companies that are taking on debt at the moment are going to face higher interest costs too. So their profits will be squeezed as well. And that's one reason why when the bond market gets sick the equity market tends to catch a cold as well."
